_comment: M7 step 7, the townspeople's talk (docs/M7-plan.md, decisions 11 and 12): each speaker's lines (the ten freed shades of data/shades.json and the Ferryman), each for a moment (first, death, won, boss, idle, reply; quest and questDone kept for step 8), with conditions on the save (`when`), what an idle line tells of (`fill`: a foe's weakness, a boss's fear, a reaction) and up to two choices, each leading to a reply and setting flags. Read and checked by src/vigil/dialogueData.ts. Placeholder lines within the lore limits, the owner's to rewrite.

lines.text: Free, and standing on stone that doesn't hum. I called the storms over the pass once. Down there I called nothing; they chained me for trying.
The Wardens' own wards. Their stone drinks a spark and keeps it. Strike the locks with what they ask for, and they let go.
They always wait. That's the trouble with storms.
{struck}. I felt the air go still when it struck you. Next time, strike first and let the thunder follow.
The War-Tiger. Its plates shed water and fire alike, but a shock through rime cracks them. Ice first, then lightning.
You saw the sky. Was there weather? Tell me there was weather.
{boss} is down. The halls breathe easier; I can hear them.
Lightning loves standing water. Shock a pool and everything wading in it learns that too.
Spilled oil, set alight, then a spark through it: the whole floor answers. Stand well back.
Arc leaps from foe to foe. Mark one first, and the mark leaps with it.
The old one with the leaves in his beard says storms are only rain with a temper. He is wrong, and he knows it.
Ah. Light, and no roots in my wrists. I grew things, once, in the high forests where the clouds sit. Down there even the moss had forgotten how.
Everything can grow anywhere. Overgrow a foe and its roots will hold it; set those roots alight and see what blooms.
Friends. A good word. It grows slowly, and lasts.
{struck} cut you down. Seeds fall too, and come up again in spring. So do you, it seems.
Daylight! On your skin, real daylight. Did anything green grow at the cave mouth? Even a little?
{boss} has gone to the dark it came from. Good. Let the floor be quiet a while.
There are gardens below, gone wild. Their flowers burst at a touch and tangle every foe near them. Break one in a fight.
A hex on an overgrown foe rots the vines into blight. Ugly work, but it spreads.
Holy light on fresh growth makes it flower, and a flower mends what's hurt. Remember that when you're bleeding.
One of the ways out of here is a dead root through the wall. I could wake it, if my hands remembered how. Yours might.
I came down after a lost goat, if you'll believe it. The goat got out. I didn't. I know the creatures below, though. Ask me.
Every one of them fears something: fire, cold, a spark, holy light, the dark. Watch what makes them flinch. Come back and I'll tell you what I saw.
Home in the valleys by now, fat and pleased with itself. Goats always win.
{struck} got you. I know that one. Next time, watch how it moves before it moves.
The crypt spiders hang where you can't see them. Look up when the threads catch the light, and burn the webs.
You came up into the valleys? Did you smell the grass? Down here I forgot what grass smells like.
{boss}! I watched it from my chains. I'm glad it's still.
The {foe}: I watched it a long while. It fears {school}. Try it.
The rime wolves hunt in packs and take turns at you. Fire scatters them.
Foes leave bits of themselves behind: moss, salt, dust. Dr. Jelly brews them into potions, if you bring him two.
Oh. Oh, the ink is dry. I copied the Wardens' grimoires once, page after page. They chained me in the burning scriptorium, with the books. I remember every page.
Then listen. A spell is never alone: what one leaves behind, another can strike. That is the whole of magic, and most mages never learn it.
Paper burns. What was written stays, if someone remembers it. I do.
{struck}. I shall write it down, so we don't forget. Next time it won't be so easy for it.
You reached the top of the pass. I shall write that down too, in the largest letters I have.
{boss}, put to rest. A good chapter. Short, but good.
Have you tried {a} and {b} on one foe together? The books call it {reaction}. Set it off and see.
Cast into what another spell left: lightning through holy ground, fire across a hexed floor. The books call those weaves.
Every floor has a library, a quiet room at the end of a passage. Its lecterns hold pages; a page teaches a spell.
A rune carved into a spell changes how it's cast: thrice, wider, longer. Waystones carve them, past each floor's keeper.
Hm. Up here, then. I dug graves for the Wardens' dead, and some of their living. I know where the walls are thin. Every floor has a room it's hiding.
Behind cracked walls. Strike a wall with a bolt: if it rings hollow, there's a room behind. A glyph's blast opens it.
Don't thank a sexton. Bad luck. Just come back up, that's thanks enough.
{struck}, was it. I've buried better than you, mage, and they stayed buried. You don't. I like that.
The room itself had you. Pits, fire, spikes. The dead don't hate you; their rooms do.
Out in the daylight, and not on a bier. That's a first for me to see.
{boss}. I'd have dug it a grave, if it had ever been the kind to lie in one.
The hollow walls ring to a bolt. Listen as you go. Once a floor, there's a cell behind one: some forgotten mage's, and what they left.
The vaults take a bone key. No key? Two glyphs at the door will force it, but it wakes the vault's warden.
Urns hold obols, mostly. The ones with runes on them hold more, and sometimes something that bites.
I had a keyring once. Opened any vault. If you find it below, it's yours. Don't tell the Wardens.
I sang the hours in the Wardens' chapel. Down in the dark, I kept singing; it's why they chained me. Bosses hear song, you know. They listen for it.
Later. When the candles are all lit. I'll sing then, and you'll hear the whole Vigil answer.
Each fears one school more than the others. Meet them, and I'll tell you what I heard them flinch at.
{struck} silenced you. Only for a while. You're singing again already; I can hear it.
Was there birdsong? At the cave mouth, in the morning? Hum it for me, if you can.
{boss} is quiet now. I'll sing it something, so it isn't quiet alone.
{boss}: in my chains I heard it fight. It flinched at {school} every time.
The choir larks sing the foes round them faster. A hex hushes them. I'm not proud of my cousins.
In the chapels below, light every candle and the next spells you cast are blessed. The Wardens liked their candles lit.
Is that the bell? No. My ears still ring. I rang the Gate's bells above the pass, before I went below. Bells there still answer a blast.
A bolt rings them, a blast louder. A bell rung beside the pillars brings down the dragon that coils on them.
They never rest. But thank you.
{struck}. I rang for you, down there, when I felt you fall. You'll not have heard it.
The Gate! Did its bells ring as you came up? They should have. They always rang for the living.
{boss} fell. Someone should ring for it. I'll do it quietly.
The Pillar Dragon. Did you ring the belfry's bells at it? That's what they're there for.
{boss} hates {school}. I watched it from the dark, ringing my chains.
The watching statues mark where you stand before they strike. Hex their eyes and they lose you.
I was only a novice. I took a candle down to see. They chained me for that. I know the dark down there, the way you know a room you grew up in.
Things that hide in shadow and come out when the lights go. Keep a light near you, and the dark keeps its distance.
I was curious. It's not the same. But it's kind of you.
{struck}. I'm sorry. Did it hurt? It hurts less each time, they say. I don't believe them.
Your own glyph? Oh. Oh no. Stand further back next time. I won't tell anyone.
You went all the way out. I'll go one day too. Not yet. One day.
{boss}! Is it really gone? I'll stop being afraid of it, then.
Kaelith knelt to you? The Shadow Sentinel? Then the seal is yours to keep now. That's frightening, and wonderful.
{boss}: the others whispered it fears {school}. I'm telling you; don't tell them I told.
A hex drains your mana if it lands on you. If it does, cast holy light after; some of it comes back.
Air. Clean air, no salts, no resins. I prepared the Wardens' dead below. Draughts, tinctures. Some kept the dead still. Some woke them.
Two reagents and a table: that's all a potion is. Dr. Jelly has the table. Bring him what foes leave behind.
The Grave Draught. Throw it at a foe and it fights for you, for a while. Don't drink it.
{struck}. I'd have prepared you properly, but you keep getting up. Good. Saves salt.
You came up whole. Not a scratch to bind. I hardly know what to do with my hands.
{boss} is dead. Truly dead, I mean. I can tell these things.
Each run the bottles look different. The first time you drink one, you'll know it. Or throw it, and watch.
Every potion can be drunk or thrown, and none does the same thing both ways. Try each both ways, once.
You've brewed before. Good. Bone dust and rimewater, try that, if you haven't.
I walked to the Gate of Uzulim to see the Wardens, and I kept walking, down and down. I've seen every floor. Shall I tell you what's below?
Five floors, then the Seal. Each one walls off a school; each one teaches its own counter. I'll tell you of the next you haven't seen.
Because the way went on. That's all a pilgrim needs. You know that feeling, I think.
{struck}. The way is long. Rest, then walk it again.
Kaelith stopped you at the Seal. It stopped me too. Strike each of its wards with its own school.
You walked out through the Pass of Buluiain at dawn. The road goes on from there, you know. It always does.
{boss} lies still on the way. One step lighter.
Below the Ossuary, the Drowned Catacombs: water everywhere. Freeze it and walk on it; shock it and everything in it suffers.
Deeper, the Burning Scriptorium, where the books still burn. Bring frost. The fire foes fear little else.
Then the Gilded Reliquary. Take the gold, and the treasury's guardians wake. Holy things there fear the dark.
Then the Ferryman's Shore, where the dead wait to cross. What waits in the dark there fears holy light.
Below the shore, the Seal, and Kaelith before it. It doesn't want to fight you. It will anyway.
Every floor's way down lies past a waystone, beside where its keeper falls. Rest there before you go on.
You'll go down again. They all do, the ones who wake here. Step aboard when you're ready. The first landing asks nothing.
An obol on the eyes, up above. Down here, the dead have no more use for theirs. Keep yours.
No one is. Step aboard anyway.
{struck}. I saw you come back across. You looked surprised. They always do.
You went up and out, and still you came back here. Most don't. I am glad of the company.
The water is still today. It always is. That is the only thing about it I trust.
Every shade you free comes up here past my boat. I don't charge them. Don't tell anyone.
The coins are cold. Good. I remember the last storm I called over the pass: the Wardens' banners stood straight out, and not one of them fell.
I remember my name being shouted over the thunder, and laughing. Take this too: the mantle I wore in the storm, the way I wore it.
Ah. I remember the clouds coming down through the trees each morning, and the moss drinking them. Everything green was listening.
I remember the seeds I carried down, in case. Here: the pollen that was in them. It still knows how to wake.
Five obols for a forager? I remember my mother counting coins like these, laughing at how few they were.
I remember the valleys at harvest, every basket full. I'll bring back twice as much for you now. I know where to look.
I remember the smell of the ink, oak gall and soot, and the first page I copied without a blot.
I remember a page I hid from the Wardens, because it was too beautiful to burn. I'll leave one like it for you, every descent.
Coins on the eyes. I put plenty there myself. I remember every name I cut into stone; there were a great many.
I remember the key I kept for the vault doors, on a nail behind the chapel. Take a key down with you each time; it's what I'd do.
I remember the first time my voice filled the whole chapel, and the candles leaned towards it.
I remember the hymn for the holy ground, the one the Wardens sang before they cut a grave. I'll teach it to you: it was a spell all along.
I remember the weight of the rope, and how the bell answered a moment late, every time, like an old friend.
I remember a soul who sat by my bell every evening and never spoke. It goes with you now, a pale light at your side.
I remember my first candle, how it shook. And then how it stopped shaking.
I remember the hands in the dark, holding, not hurting. I learned how to call them. Now you can.
I remember the jars in their rows, every one labelled in my hand. The Wardens trusted no one else with them.
I remember my best recipes. Not the polite ones. Take them; they'll serve you better than they served the dead.
I remember the first stone of the road, worn into a bowl by all the feet before mine.
I remember walking out onto a frozen lake and the ice holding. That's a wall you can carry. Take it.
Then take what I kept for the long nights: a deeper well of ink. You'll find more mana in you, every descent.
Here. A heart I dug up and never gave back. It beats well enough. It's yours, in every descent.
A stick of chalk from the bell tower. It never runs short of one glyph. Take it down with you each time.
I'll cut a second socket into your first spell, the way the Wardens taught us. Every descent, it will be there.
A pilgrim's purse, five obols in it, always five. Don't ask me how. Take it every time you go down.
A phial, always full of something. I fill it while you sleep. You'll go down with a potion every time.
I lost my keyring down there, on its nail behind some vault door. If you ever carry it back up, I'll know.
My keyring! You brought it up. Here: a hallowed light I kept by my lantern. It goes with you now, every descent.
Three reactions you've never seen, mage. Go and set them off, and come back and tell me how they looked.
Three new ones! Wonderful. I've carved a rune for you to carry, a new one each descent. Write to me in it.
Walk all the way down to the Seal. Not to fight; to see it. Then come back and tell me the road was real.
You walked it. The road was real. Then I'll give you what I know of the first floor: its every turn, before you take it.
